title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which scammers used AI-generated images and deepfake video to create a false identity for a named, living professional. The failure is not a malfunction of a product built by a legitimate company, but a deliberate misuse of AI generation tools to produce convincing likeness material at scale. The deployment point was social media, where thousands of fake profiles were created and then funneled victims to private messaging channels before collecting payment.

The scale, nearly 6,500 fake profiles removed across multiple platforms, shows that existing platform detection systems did not catch the content quickly or consistently. Catching this kind of impersonation earlier would have required either automated detection of synthetic media combined with identity-matching checks, or faster human review in response to reports. Neither appears to have operated at the speed the volume of profiles demanded.

What is not established is who the scammers are, where they operate, or whether any law enforcement action has produced findings, arrests, or charges.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are creating fake videos and social media profiles in his name. Criminals are using AI-generated images and deepfake videos to impersonate Leal and defraud vulnerable immigrants, offering fraudulent immigration services like US residency assistance for thousands of dollars. The scams typically direct victims through social media to WhatsApp, where fraudsters send fake contracts and collect payments via apps like Venmo and Zelle.

The problem escalated dramatically over the past three months, though Leal first noticed suspicious activity in October. His office hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scam's origins. He warns immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to be cautious of requests for immediate payment through digital payment apps.
